pending_articles.title: A phase decoder for reconstructing missing muscle activity
pending_articles.content: Upper-limb assistive devices are commonly controlled with electromyographic (EMG) signals, but nerve injury, muscle loss, or practical limits on electrode placement can leave only a few usable signals, which constrains the decoding of intended movements. Here, we introduce a decoder that reconstructs missing muscle activations from sparse EMGs using a two-stage real-time approach: (1) estimating ongoing movement phase from available signals, and (2) retrieving corresponding muscle activations from a library of pre-recorded muscle activity templates. In proof-of-concept tests, neurologically intact participants (N=4) performed object-transfer tasks under simulated denervation conditions. The decoder accurately estimated movement phase (median root-mean-square error [RMSE] <0.17 of movement duration) and reconstructed missing muscle activations (RMSE 0.08-0.34; correlation up to 0.97) within ~2 ms, in a previously unseen participant. The results indicate that template based reconstruction could leverage sparse EMG for low latency control of assistive technology.
pending_articles.author: Bahdasariants, S., Yakovenko, S.

pending_articles.title: State-dependent emergence of coupling between oscillatory and aperiodic neural activity
pending_articles.content: Neural oscillations and aperiodic activity are two quintessential mesoscopic-level features arising from shared circuits, yet what governs their relationship remains unclear. Here we show that coupling between oscillatory frequency and aperiodic exponent is sporadic and state-dependent. Bias-reduced analyses of 3,245 intracranial contacts from 61 awake subjects showed significant coupling in only <13% of contacts per band. A connectome-constrained dynamical model predicted that neither changes of input to local circuit nor removal of long-range connections modulated the coupling; whereas stronger local inhibitory feedback drove covariation between oscillatory frequency and aperiodic exponent. The model predictions were supported by three independent experiments: transcranial stimulation shifted each component independently and focal ablation of remote cortical tissues did not change coupling; whereas coupling emerged during seizures that altered local excitatory-inhibitory balance. These results suggest that the relation between periodic and aperiodic neural activity is neither intrinsically independent nor coupled, but determined by local circuit states.

pending_articles.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
pending_articles.content: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

pending_articles.title: Paraquat Inhalation Produces Male-Biased Dopaminergic Neuron Loss and Motor Deficits in Mice: Relevance to Parkinsons Disease
pending_articles.content: Long-term exposure to paraquat (PQ), a widely used herbicide, has been linked to increased risk of Parkinsons Disease (PD) in agricultural workers and rural communities in the United States (US), findings further supported by experimental animal studies. Although banned in many countries across the globe, PQ remains widely used in the US. Inhalation of PQ has been known to induce systemic organ failure at acute concentrations. However, prolonged low-dose inhalation from agricultural spraying and pesticide drift has not been readily evaluated for its potential to contribute to neurodegenerative diseases in vivo. Instead, many experimental studies have relied on systemic routes of exposure, which do not effectively replicate the most common route of exposure to PQ in the environment. In the current study, Parkinsonian features were examined in mice that had been exposed via whole-body inhalation to PQ aerosol for either 40 or 60 days. Levels of PQ in brain were highest in olfactory bulb, followed by frontal cortex and then brainstem in both sexes. After 60 days of exposure, male-specific impairments in locomotor activity were observed, in addition to reductions in striatal dopamine, in substantia nigra tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and number of TH+ dopaminergic neurons, the latter being considered the primary basis of PD, along with increased olfactory bulb -synuclein levels. As such, these studies confirm the dopaminergic neurotoxicity of inhaled PQ. These findings raise significant concerns as to the contribution of PQ exposures to the continued increase in the incidence of PD in the US.

pending_articles.title: Imipramine binds to amyloid-β and extends the survival of Alzheimer's disease patients
pending_articles.content: Background Apolipoprotein E (apoE) plays numerous roles in the pathogenic pathway to Alzheimer's disease (AD). We previously performed a high-throughput screen and identified the antidepressant imipramine as an inhibitor of the interaction between apoE and amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}). We also found that imipramine use to treat depression in AD patients was associated with better Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) scores. Here we studied the mechanisms by which imipramine inhibits the AD pathogenic pathway and investigated its effect on mortality in AD patients. Methods Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used to characterize the interaction between imipramine and A{beta} monomers. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived AD cerebral organoids (COs) and transgenic AD rats treated with imipramine underwent neuropathological evaluation, while rat learning and memory were assessed in the Morris Water Maze. AD patient mortality in the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center's database was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Imipramine inhibits the apoE-A{beta} interaction by binding directly to A{beta} monomers. Imipramine reduces A{beta} accumulation and neuronal cell loss in AD COs. Imipramine-treated female AD rats had enhanced reference memory and increased hippocampal cellularity and cholinergic neurotransmission. AD patients prescribed imipramine had reduced all-cause mortality over 10 years relative to those prescribed other tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), non-TCA antidepressants, or no antidepressants. Conclusions The findings support the conclusions that: a) the mechanism by which apoE confers risk for AD is by catalyzing the polymerization of A{beta} into neurotoxic species, b) targeting apoE is a promising, underappreciated strategy for the prevention of AD, c) imipramine should be used more frequently to treat depression in AD clinical practice, and d) imipramine should be evaluated in prospective trials, particularly in APOE4 carriers, as a potential method to improve cognition and reduce mortality in AD.

pending_articles.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
pending_articles.content: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

pending_articles.title: Hmox1/CO regulates retina regeneration via modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling and induction of vaspb in zebrafish
pending_articles.content: Muller glia (MG) in the zebrafish retina retain a latent stem cell capacity that is absent in mammals, yet the injury responsive signals that drive this reprogramming remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), the stress-inducible, rate-limiting enzyme of heme catabolism, as a previously unrecognized regulator of this process. Following injury, hmox1a is selectively and rapidly induced among the heme oxygenase gene family, localizing to photoreceptors with expression peaking during the MG proliferation window. Pharmacological inhibition and morpholino mediated knockdown of Hmox1 dysregulate the acute inflammatory response, impair Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) proliferation, and produce lasting deficits in retinal lamination, establishing Hmox1 as a potentially non-redundant, early-acting node required for structural recovery. Exogenous delivery of carbon monoxide (CO), a bioactive Hmox1 metabolite, partially rescues each of these phenotypes, functionally implicating CO as a key downstream effector. Mechanistically, Hmox1/CO signalling stabilizes {beta}-catenin likely via transcriptional repression of the Wnt antagonist dkk1b. This stabilized {beta}-catenin is enriched at a predicted Tcf7l2 site in the promoter of vaspb, which encodes an actin binding protein and is newly identified here as an injury-induced Wnt target gene. Bioinformatic and functional analyses further implicate Nfe2l2a (Nrf2) as a candidate intermediary bridging Hmox1/CO to Wnt regulation, with putative antioxidant response elements identified within the dkk1b locus. Together, these findings outline a putative Hmox1[->]CO[->]Nrf2[->]dkk1b[->]{beta}-catenin[->]vaspb relay coupling redox biology to Wnt-dependent glial reprogramming. Notably, HO-1 is similarly induced in stressed mammalian retina, yet Wnt/{beta}-catenin activation fails to sustain regeneration, positioning the Hmox1/CO axis as a candidate target for future investigation in mammalian retina regeneration.

recently_processed.title: Brief Peppermint Odour Exposure and Immediate Free Recall of a Visual Object Array: A Three-Arm Randomised Experiment
recently_processed.content: Background: Odours reach limbic and prefrontal targets through a uniquely direct pathway and are often claimed to enhance cognition, yet experimental evidence for specific essential oils is mixed and frequently confounded by expectancy. We tested whether a brief inhalation of peppermint or clove essential oil, compared with no odour, alters immediate free recall of a visual object array. Methods: Sixty healthy adults aged 18-50 years were randomly allocated to peppermint oil, clove oil or no odour (n = 20 each). After 30 s of inhalation (or none), participants studied a 4 x 4 array of 16 pictured items for 20 s and then wrote down every item they could recall, without time limit. Groups were compared with one-way and Welch ANOVA, Welch-corrected pairwise tests with Holm correction, Hedges' g with 95% confidence intervals and Bayes factors. Results: Recall differed across conditions (Welch F(2, 37.0) = 8.53, p < .001; omega2 = 0.14). Participants exposed to peppermint recalled more items (11.20 +/- 2.14) than those exposed to no odour (8.45 +/- 2.04; g = 1.29, 95% CI [0.61, 1.97], p(Holm) < .001, BF10 = 134). Clove (9.55 +/- 3.19) did not differ reliably from either no odour (g = 0.40, p(Holm) = .203) or peppermint (g = 0.60, p(Holm) = .127; BF10 = 1.29). Conclusions: A single brief exposure to peppermint oil was associated with substantially better immediate recall than no odour. Because the peppermint-clove contrast was inconclusive and no placebo odour was used, the data do not establish an odour-specific effect; general arousal and expectancy remain plausible contributors. Pre-registered, laboratory-based replications with placebo odours, blinding and arousal measures are required.
recently_processed.author: Akar, B., Altıntas, T.

recently_processed.title: Myelin Governs Hippocampal Network Function through the Extracellular Space it Occupies, Not Only the Axons it Insulates
recently_processed.content: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Beyond electrical insulation, myelin occupies volume, and therefore shapes the extracellular space (ECS) through which interstitial fluid flows and neurotransmitter diffuses. How these two roles interact is unknown. We built a multi-scale model of hippocampal CA1 coupling lattice Boltzmann simulations of ECS flow to detailed networks of reconstructed neurons and glia. Demyelination enlarged the ECS volume fraction from 28 to 43 per cent up to 43 to 70 per cent across layers, lowered tortuosity from about 1.7 to 1.4, raised effective diffusivity from 0.35 to 0.50 of free solution and shortened solute breakthrough times by roughly a third, while raising flow speed yet lowering viscous dissipation. Because transmitter concentration scales inversely with that volume, synaptic driving force fell: postsynaptic potential amplitude declined with wrap count and transmission failed entirely below four of sixteen wraps. In 200-cell networks, demyelination halved firing (pyramidal 7.9 to 4.4 Hz), rendered discharge burst-dominated, reduced band power by up to 8.7-fold and displaced the population state, which a classifier separated at 100 per cent accuracy, whereas an inflammatory glial census left every functional measure unchanged. Driving myelin continuously from intact to 12.5 per cent and back recovered the same threshold near four wraps, and firing rate and spectral power returned fully to baseline. Myelin thus governs circuit function through the space it vacates as well as the axons it insulates, with opposite consequences for clearance and for signalling, a dissociation that may matter in demyelinating disease.
